title: Lab 1 — Quiz 3
subtitle: Biochemistry review videos — pH, buffers, macromolecules

questions.prompt: A solution with a pH of 3 is:
questions.explanation: pH below 7 = acidic; 7 = neutral; above 7 = basic.

why.A: Basic (alkaline) solutions have a pH above 7.
why.D: A buffer resists pH change; pH 3 simply describes acidity.

options.text: Releases hydrogen ions to lower pH
Accepts hydrogen ions to raise pH

questions.explanation: Buffers resist pH changes — that's why they are added to culture media to keep the pH appropriate.

questions.prompt: An acid is a substance that:
questions.explanation: Acids donate H+ (pH below 7); bases accept H+ or release OH- (pH above 7).

questions.prompt: What are the four classes of macromolecules essential to cells?
questions.explanation: The 4 classes of biomolecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

why.A: Vitamins aren't one of the four macromolecule classes.
why.B: Salts and water are not macromolecules.
why.D: Enzymes and many hormones are proteins, not separate classes.

questions.prompt: What is the monomer (building block) of proteins?
questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

why.D: Fatty acids (with glycerol) build lipids like triglycerides.

questions.prompt: What is the monomer of carbohydrates?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides (simple sugars such as glucose).

questions.prompt: Which is a major function of carbohydrates?

options.text: Forming the bilayer of cell membranes

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates supply energy (e.g., glucose), store energy (starch, glycogen) and provide structure (e.g., cellulose, peptidoglycan).

questions.prompt: Phospholipids are important to cells because they:

options.text: Form the bilayer of cell membranes

questions.explanation: Phospholipids form membranes; triglycerides store energy long-term and insulate.

questions.prompt: What are the three components of a nucleotide?

options.text: An amino group, a carboxyl group, and an R group
A phosphate, a fatty acid, and a sugar
A phosphate, a sugar, and a nitrogenous base

questions.explanation: Each nucleotide = phosphate + 5-carbon sugar (deoxyribose or ribose) + nitrogenous base.

why.A: Those make up an amino acid.
why.C: Nucleotides contain a nitrogenous base, not a fatty acid.

questions.prompt: Which list shows the 5 nitrogenous bases found in DNA and RNA?
questions.explanation: A, G, C are in both; T is in DNA only; U is in RNA only.

why.A: Ribose is a sugar, not a base.
why.C: Phosphate isn't a base; guanine is missing.

options.text: The bond that joins two amino acids
The bond that joins two nucleotides
The bond between paired DNA bases
The bond joining fatty acids to glycerol

questions.explanation: A peptide bond links amino acids into a polypeptide.

why.B: Nucleotides are joined by sugar–phosphate (covalent) bonds.
why.C: Base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds.

questions.prompt: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids?
questions.explanation: Primary = amino acid sequence; secondary = alpha helices/beta sheets; tertiary = 3-D shape; quaternary = 2+ polypeptides combined.

why.B: Secondary structure is folding into helices and sheets.
why.C: Tertiary is the overall 3-D folding of one chain.
why.D: Quaternary is multiple chains joined together.

questions.prompt: A protein made of two or more polypeptide chains joined together shows which level of structure?
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure involves more than one polypeptide chain.

why.B: Secondary is helices and pleated sheets.
why.D: Tertiary is the 3-D shape of a single chain.

options.text: Loss of a protein's shape, and therefore its function
Joining amino acids with peptide bonds
Breaking a protein into individual amino acids

questions.explanation: High temperature, extreme pH and high salt can denature proteins — they unfold and stop working.

why.C: Denaturation unfolds the protein; it doesn't break peptide bonds.

questions.prompt: Which is a function of proteins?
questions.explanation: Proteins act as enzymes, transporters, structural components, antibodies and more.
